intro: According to its colophon, this New Script tablet holds two rituals. The first, by Puliša (§0–6), is for a plague that breaks out after the king has campaigned in an enemy land: a prisoner of war and a woman, then a bull and a ewe, are dressed up as substitutes for the male or female enemy deity who caused it and sent back to the enemy land. The second, the fragmentary ritual of the woman Ummaya (§7–12), includes a long Hurrian incantation that names Muršili.

sections.title: Ritual of Puliša against plague from an enemy land
Ritual of Ummaya, with Hurrian incantation, and colophon

paras.en: Thus (says) Puliša: (If the king) strikes an enemy land, a[nd he] goes [away from the border of the enemy land], and a plague arises among mankind, (caused by) either some male deity [or a female deity], [then I do as follows]:

When he goes away from the border of the enemy land, they seize one prisoner of war and one woman of the land. On [whatever road] the king came from the enemy land, onto that road the king st[eps], and all the lords step (in) behind him. They bring one prisoner and one woman before him. (The king) takes the festive garments off his body, and they clothe the man in them; the woman they clothe in the festive garments of a woman. Then the king speaks to the man as follows — but if it is [not] convenient for the king, he sends another, and that one takes over the ritual and speaks to the man as follows —: 'If some male deity of the enemy land has caused this plague, see, I have given him an adorned man as his substitute. This one is great in the head, this one is great in the heart, and this one is great in the loins. You, male deity, be fully appeased with th[is] adorned man! But towards the king, [the lords], the ar[my and] the land of Ḫatti turn again in favour! […] let this prisoner li[ft up] the plague and carry it back [into the enemy land]!'
But to the woman he speaks (the words) about a female deity; […] exactly the same.

Afterwards they drive up one bull and one [ewe] of the enemy land itself, and he …s him (the bull) fitted with ašuša-(rings?) at his ears. Red wool, green wool, black wool (and) [white wool] he draws out of the king's mouth, [and speaks as follows]: 'Because(?) the king keeps turning red, turning yellow, turning dark [and wasting away(?)], that […] back to the enemy land […]. And the king's person, the lords, the troops (and) the horses it does [not](?) know; it knows(?) those of the enemy land […]' […] he places, and it […] on the emmer […]. [Then] the ašuša-(ringed) [bull] […] [and] he speaks [as follows]: 'Whatever god of [enmity] has [caused this plague] — if he is a male deity, (see,) I have given you an [adorned], ašuša-(ringed), approved(?) [bull]. [You, male deity,] be fully appeased, and [let this bull] carry [this plague] back into the enemy land! [But towards the king, the princes,] the lords, the army and the la[nd of Ḫatti turn again in favour]!'
Afterwards (they bring) the adorned ewe, and he speaks (the words) about a female deity, [exactly the same].
Then they drive the ašuša-(ringed) bull [and the ewe] ahead of [the prisoner] and the woman.
Afterwards again […] [— break at the end of column I —] which(?) […] from […] let [it] carry […] good again […]
Thus (says) Umm[aya]: […] or inside the house […] swears(?), and […] the robes up […] and as follows […]

One chariot, horses, mu[les](?) […] in front, a whip […] for the hand(?), with […] […] in front, sealed(?) […] with cloth, a shirt […], BAR.DUL-garments, BAR.[…]-garments […] and a dagger stuck(?) on it […] of a woman, and that one […] […] a BAR.SI head-covering […] inside […] [— break —] […] and […] and […] and on them […] I throw down(?).

And to the king […] as substitute(?) […] […] ḫatalkešna-(hawthorn) […] and them […] […] […] [— break —] Afterwards […] at the (city) wall I prepare (it). I take […], and over it, on the ground, I conjure.
[Hurrian incantation, not translated; it names the Storm-god Teššub, the gods, the rivers, the mountains, the earth and heaven, and Muršili.]
[Hurrian incantation, continued, not translated; it names deities, among them one called Ninuwaḫi (the one 'of Nineveh'?), again names Muršili, and mentions arrow(s) and bow.]

When he finishes the incantation, he releases the […]-man as a nakkušši-(substitute carrier), (and) two oxen […] [fo]r the Tutelary Deity he rel[eases] as nakkušši-(substitute carriers); […] he goes. [Colophon, on the left edge:] On the tablet (are) two rituals: the ritual of Puliša; the ritual of Ummaya. […]
